report:
## Conclusion: The claim is well-supported by high-quality evidence.

Add-on cannabidiol (CBD) does reduce convulsive seizure frequency in children with Dravet syndrome, and this is one of the best-established findings in modern epilepsy pharmacotherapy.

**Pivotal trial:** The landmark evidence comes from a multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (Devinsky et al., 2017), which randomized 120 children and young adults with Dravet syndrome, all already on other antiepileptic drugs, to add-on CBD oral solution or placebo. Median convulsive-seizure frequency fell 38.9% with CBD versus 13.3% with placebo—a statistically significant difference (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618; summarized at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5716495/).

**Confirmatory dose-ranging trial:** A second randomized trial in JAMA Neurology (Miller et al., 2020) tested 10 mg/kg/day and 20 mg/kg/day CBD versus placebo in 199 children, finding both doses significantly reduced convulsive seizures versus placebo, with the lower dose showing a comparable benefit and better tolerability (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458).

**Long-term/safety data:** An open-label extension study confirmed sustained seizure reduction and characterized long-term safety, though adverse events (somnolence, diarrhea, elevated liver enzymes, fatigue) were more common with CBD than placebo (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/epi.14628).

This evidence base led the FDA to approve Epidiolex (purified CBD) specifically for Dravet syndrome seizures, reinforcing regulatory confidence in the finding.

**Bottom line:** Multiple independent, adequately powered randomized controlled trials, corroborated by long-term follow-up and regulatory approval, support that add-on CBD meaningfully reduces convulsive seizure frequency in Dravet syndrome, albeit with a notable side-effect burden requiring monitoring.
